Bat acoustic activity varied substantially across the sampling period, among sites, and in relation to nightly environmental conditions. Seasonal phenology differed markedly among sites, indicating substantial local variation in the timing and magnitude of activity. Temperature was positively associated with activity across all three echolocation-frequency groups, suggesting a broadly shared response to warmer nightly conditions. The clearest evidence of systematic differences among frequency groups occurred with relative humidity: low-frequency activity remained comparatively stable, mid-frequency activity declined, and high-frequency activity showed the strongest decline. This ordering matched our a priori prediction from the frequency-dependent physics of ultrasonic sound propagation. Together, these results indicate that environmental conditions can structure bat activity through processes operating at multiple temporal and biological scales, including mechanisms linked to sensory ecology.

## Seasonal phenology and nightly environmental conditions

Seasonal variation in bat activity reflected both changes in nightly environmental conditions and seasonal processes not captured by those conditions. The substantial difference between the overall and environmentally conditioned seasonal patterns indicates that the observed seasonal pattern in acoustic activity can partly reflect the strong seasonal covariance between weather and bat activity. This is consistent with studies showing that temperature and other weather conditions structure nightly bat activity across temperate systems [@benderBatActivityIncreases2015; @jorgeFireLandCover2021; @masWinterBatActivity2022; @russo-petrickIdentifyingFactorsMultiple2023; @wolbertBatActivityInsect2014]. At the same time, a pronounced seasonal signal remained after accounting for temperature, relative humidity, and lunar phase, indicating that weather alone does not account for seasonal changes in activity. Seasonal changes in bat activity can also reflect migration and redistribution across the landscape [@cryanSeasonalDistributionMigratory2003; @wellerFirstDirectEvidence2016], reproductive phenology and the energetic demands of lactation [@deeley2022], seasonal changes in roost and habitat use [@lewis2022], and temporal variation in prey availability [@metcalfe2023]. Seasonal activity should therefore be viewed not simply as a response to changing weather, but as the combined outcome of environmental conditions and biological phenology.

The strong among-site differences in seasonal phenology further demonstrate that these processes operate at local as well as regional scales. Sites exposed to the same broad climatic season nevertheless differed substantially in the timing and magnitude of activity. Local habitat conditions, proximity to roosts, resource availability, species composition, and seasonal changes in landscape use could all generate such differences. Consequently, a regional seasonal trajectory may obscure biologically meaningful spatial variation in phenology, even when monitoring sites are geographically close. This spatial heterogeneity may be particularly important in acoustic monitoring studies, where seasonal changes in the species using individual sites can produce very different local activity trajectories within the same regional bat assemblage.

Accounting for this local phenology is also important when estimating associations with nightly environmental conditions. Temperature and humidity vary seasonally at the same time that bat populations undergo changes in migration, reproduction, energetic requirements, and habitat use. Environmental associations can therefore incorporate multiple processes if seasonal structure is inadequately represented. Our results suggest that explicitly representing local seasonal trajectories can help distinguish this phenological variation from associations with nightly environmental conditions.

## Humidity and echolocation frequency

Relative humidity produced the clearest evidence that environmental sensitivity differed systematically among echolocation-frequency groups. Activity declined with increasing humidity in the mid- and high-frequency groups, with the strongest response occurring among high-frequency species, whereas activity in the low-frequency group remained comparatively stable. Thus, sensitivity to humidity increased across the frequency gradient in the direction predicted from the physical properties of ultrasonic sound propagation.

This frequency ordering is consistent with atmospheric attenuation as one mechanism contributing to the observed response. Atmospheric absorption increases strongly with ultrasonic frequency, while its relationship with humidity is nonlinear and frequency dependent [@griffinImportanceAtmosphericAttenuation1971; @lawrenceMeasurementsAtmosphericAttenuation1982]. Consequently, changes in atmospheric conditions can alter the effective sensory range available to echolocating bats, with effects that depend on call frequency. Reduced sensory range can decrease the volume of space over which prey can be detected and potentially alter foraging efficiency [@luoGlobalWarmingAlters2014]. Recent measurements from free-flying temperate bats further indicate that behavioral adjustments in echolocation calls do not necessarily compensate for weather-induced increases in attenuation and associated reductions in prey-detection distance [@deframondTemperateBatsMay2023].

Atmospheric attenuation is unlikely to be the only process linking humidity to bat activity. Relative humidity and other weather conditions can influence the flight activity and availability of nocturnal insects, including Lepidoptera [@gregg1994; @hirao2008], providing a prey-mediated pathway through which humidity could influence bat activity independently of acoustic transmission. These relationships need not be monotonic and may differ among insect taxa and environmental conditions. Species within our frequency groups also differ in ecological characteristics beyond call frequency. Nevertheless, the observed ordering is notable because it followed an a priori prediction derived from acoustic principles rather than a pattern defined after examining the activity data. Moreover, the frequency-dependent association remained after accounting for temperature and seasonal phenology. The correspondence between a mechanistic prediction about sound propagation and the observed ordering of field activity therefore provides evidence that atmospheric transmission contributes to variation in bat activity associated with humidity, while leaving open the possibility that prey dynamics and other ecological processes contribute simultaneously.

## Temperature

Temperature was strongly positively associated with activity across all three frequency groups, although the magnitude and shape of the responses differed among groups. This broadly consistent response indicates that warmer nights favored bat activity across much of the assemblage rather than producing contrasting thermal responses among groups defined by echolocation frequency.

Positive associations between temperature and bat activity are widely reported in temperate systems [@benderBatActivityIncreases2015; @jorgeFireLandCover2021; @masWinterBatActivity2022; @russo-petrickIdentifyingFactorsMultiple2023; @wolbertBatActivityInsect2014]. Temperature can influence nightly activity through several interacting pathways. Warmer conditions can increase the activity and availability of aerial insects, while also reducing the energetic costs of thermoregulation and increasing the profitability of emergence and foraging. Conversely, cool nights can simultaneously constrain prey availability and increase the energetic costs of maintaining body temperature. The positive temperature associations observed across all three frequency groups are therefore consistent with both trophic and physiological mechanisms rather than a single temperature-dependent process.

Differences among frequency groups should not, however, be interpreted as evidence that echolocation frequency itself determines thermal sensitivity. Unlike the direct physical relationship between call frequency and atmospheric attenuation, there is no comparable mechanism linking characteristic echolocation frequency to temperature response. The frequency groups used here contain species that also differ in body size, wing morphology, migratory behavior, roosting ecology, habitat use, and foraging strategy. Differences among their temperature-response curves may therefore reflect multiple dimensions of species ecology that covary with acoustic characteristics. The common increase in activity with temperature is consequently more informative than differences in the precise shapes of the group-specific responses: warmer nights were associated with greater activity throughout the assemblage, while the mechanisms and magnitude of that response likely varied among species.

## Lunar phase

Lunar phase was a weaker and less consistent correlate of activity than temperature or relative humidity. Activity increased toward the full moon in the high-frequency group, whereas responses in the low- and mid-frequency groups were comparatively weak and uncertain. Thus, lunar phase was not associated with a consistent assemblage-wide response, but instead were associated with activity in only part of the bat assemblage.

Such heterogeneity is consistent with the broader literature on lunar responses in bats. Although a meta-analysis found an overall tendency for bat activity to decrease with increasing moonlight, the magnitude of this response varied with foraging habitat and latitude [@saldana-vazquezLunarPhobiaBats2013]. Studies of temperate insectivorous bats likewise range from little or no change in overall activity [@heckerDoesMoonlightChange1999; @karlssonNoLunarPhobia2002] to more complex responses that depend on habitat, time of night, or other environmental conditions [@heckerDoesMoonlightChange1999; @milneTemporalPatternsBats2005]. These differences suggest that responses to lunar illumination depend strongly on ecological context rather than reflecting a universal avoidance of bright nights.

Several mechanisms could generate this context dependence. Increased illumination may alter exposure to visually hunting predators, but moonlight can also change the distribution or activity of insect prey and consequently where bats forage. @heckerDoesMoonlightChange1999, for example, found no overall reduction in activity with increasing moonlight but observed shifts in the vertical distribution of bat activity within forest, which they interpreted as more consistent with changes in prey distribution than with avoidance of illuminated habitat. Habitat structure and foraging strategy may therefore mediate both the costs and potential benefits of activity under brighter conditions.

The positive lunar association in our high-frequency group should similarly not be interpreted as a direct effect of echolocation frequency. Unlike the relationship between call frequency and atmospheric attenuation, there is no clear physical mechanism predicting greater lunar sensitivity at higher echolocation frequencies. Instead, frequency groups contain species that differ in habitat use, foraging strategy, morphology, and other ecological characteristics that may influence responses to lunar illumination. Our results therefore reinforce the view that lunar effects on bat activity are assemblage- and context-dependent, with the response of particular groups potentially reflecting the ecology of their constituent species rather than echolocation frequency itself.

## Ecological implications

The contrasting responses among frequency groups indicate that environmental conditions can restructure nightly bat activity through multiple mechanisms operating simultaneously. Temperature was positively associated with activity throughout the assemblage, consistent with broad effects on bat energetics and prey availability, whereas humidity produced a distinctly frequency-ordered response consistent with differences in ultrasonic transmission. Lunar responses were weaker and less consistent among groups. Environmental conditions may therefore alter not only the overall level of bat activity but also the relative activity of species with different sensory and ecological characteristics, even within the same landscape.

The frequency-dependent humidity response suggests that changes in atmospheric conditions could affect components of bat assemblages differently. If atmospheric conditions impose greater sensory constraints on species using higher-frequency echolocation calls, variation in the frequency, magnitude, or duration of humid conditions could alter the conditions under which different components of an assemblage forage effectively. These effects would occur alongside temperature-mediated changes in prey availability and energetic costs and broader seasonal changes in migration, reproduction, and habitat use. Environmental variation may consequently alter the relative activity of species as well as total assemblage activity.

More broadly, our results demonstrate the value of linking environmental associations to mechanistic predictions about species traits. Echolocation frequency provided an independently defined characteristic from which we could predict differences in sensitivity to atmospheric conditions, and the observed humidity response increased across frequency groups in the direction predicted from the physics of ultrasonic attenuation. Atmospheric attenuation cannot be isolated from prey responses, species ecology, or environmentally structured variation in acoustic detection in an observational study, but the correspondence between an a priori mechanistic prediction and the field response provides evidence that atmospheric transmission contributes to environmental variation in bat activity. Environmental responses of bat assemblages may therefore depend not only on the conditions animals experience, but also on the sensory systems through which they interact with those conditions.
